translation: Aristotle, and likewise Theophrastus too, have stated precisely what one must look to in supposing a nature to be either well-tempered or of bad temperament; but these men do not even know this, and when they hear them saying that the animal is moist and hot, or that the mixture of the child is moist and hot, they neither understand how these things are meant, and they senselessly transfer the account to the seasons, as though it were the same thing and did not differ greatly whether one's own mixture is moist and hot or that of the air surrounding us; for it is not the same thing, nor is the mixture of an animal called moist and hot in the same way as the mixture of air is called moist and hot. What the cause of all these things was I shall now relate, and I shall show clearly to those willing to pay attention how small errors in the...

...the same thing, either to evacuate some moisture that is scattered in certain regions, or to render one's own mixture drier. For in inflamed parts there arises a certain uneven bad temperament, the homoeomerous bodies not yet having departed from their own nature but still being changed and altered, while all the intervening regions are filled with the flux. All things, then, that are hot and moist in mixture, when applied to parts so disposed, evacuate that superfluity which has occupied the intervening regions of the homoeomerous bodies, but are so far from drying the bodies themselves that they even add moisture to them. The truth, then, is thus; but what has been said needs a demonstration, which, since I consider it both too long to be appended in the present discourse and, further, to require a hearer who understands the power of drugs, I postpone, at least...

...indeed, and with rose cerate it helps greatly against these; for which conditions, indeed, and for such conditions many other drugs will also be described in the following discourse, some having a power similar to the phoenicine, others even more active. But against conditions subject to a discharge or flux this is the best drug of all, and it has often accomplished something beyond hope. When once, then, a thigh had suppurated near the groin, the inflammation over the whole of it being unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors flowed out toward the groin and through the ulcer that had formed; and when this had gone on for a longer time, the flux that had settled into the thigh was evacuated, but a certain fistulous condition developed beneath the skin along the whole thigh, so that I wished to cut it open near the kneecap, in order that there might be an outflow for the ichors from both sides...

...concerning nourishment, that the bad and the not-bad are spoken of as in relation to something, and evidently the harmful and the beneficial. For it is in another sense that you would say the Attalic plaster is better than this one, in that it is of more manifold use. Indeed Asclepiades himself, writing next after this one now described that very plaster made with white pepper, does not call it Attalic but Pamphilion, being ignorant, as I think, of the man who first discovered it, and having added the name of the man who used it and gave it to him. At any rate he wrote its promise word for word thus: 'Another, called Pamphilion, a well-tried drug; it acts on old and hard-to-heal [ulcers], carbuncles, epinyctides, achores, conditions of the nature of the itch; it glues together sinuses; it acts on abscesses, condylomata; and the drug is of almost more manifold use.' And he says it is composed of white lead...

...let each of these be done precisely for the sake of contributing something to the whiteness of the drug. And concerning the white lead it has been said before, and concerning the oil, and the manner of the boiling, and the surrounding air, and the fire, how each of them may contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the case of the others, so also in the case of these, one who knows the powers of water and of vinegar and of sea-water and of the whitest wine must mix into the composition what is most useful for the condition being treated. For in the case of ulcers with raised edges, which have lips that are thick and hard and in need of much thinning, those [metallic ingredients] triturated with vinegar and sea-water are more useful than those with water; but in cases where the moisture carried in the ulcers is acrid and biting, they should rather be triturated in water...

...each of the metallic [ingredients], just as, again, rather in wine in cases where the moisture flowing onto the ulcers appears abundant. Each of these, then, that I have mentioned, triturated for several days in each of the liquids mentioned, I added on each occasion to the drugs made of white lead and litharge, and I found by trial that all of them cicatrize most excellently; and I also gave some of the prescriptions to friends who were in need of such drugs, by whom too, when brought to the test, they appeared to preserve their promise. So when the litharge has been boiled beforehand, as has been said, with the white lead, and the drug has come near to a non-staining consistency, one must add larch or terebinth resin of the pine with white wax, and when these have been well united, add in the metallic [ingredients] in the following proportion: of litharge and of white lead, in the customary manner, a litra of each with two litrai of oil; let it be boiled many times...

...but if something scirrhous of its inflammation should remain, to apply some of the agents that dry sufficiently. Since, then, something appeared to be lacking, I first used the drug made with the root of dracontium, which in all other respects has the same ingredients as the Egyptian drug called Isis, but has in addition the root of dracontium; and next after this, having used the one called Athena, I passed from that one to the cicatrizing agents for the remainder. In another case, smearing the bared parts of the wound with the troche made with boiled-down must, dissolved, I applied euphorbium on the outside, having mixed it with wax and resin of the pine in such quantity that it should both become plaster-like and at the same time preserve the power of the euphorbium. How one who looks to these aims should compound the drug I shall say next; for indeed I also made another drug with vinegar...

...just as to resin of the pine and to pitch; for this reason I mix with the cerate resin of the pine, or pitch, or a portion of each. It is quite evident, then, that when these are mixed the oil is no longer to be put in equal to them; for wax needs much of the fat to attain moistness, whereas the resins of the pine, the dry ones, need altogether little, and the moist ones even want to take on some dry substance to attain a plaster-like consistency. Among waxes, then, there is no great difference in respect of moistness and dryness; but with the resins of the pine, conversely, as also with pitch, the difference between the dry ones and the moist ones is very great. The driest of the resins of the pine, then, is the one that some call roasted, others colophony; second is the one from the pottery-works, impure and unroasted; but if one purifies it...

...you have seen me doing throughout, not in the case of this one alone but also of ammoniac incense. The drug written after this by the Tarentine is also of the same promise, in the following proportion: of chalcitis 25 drachmas, of cadmia 12 drachmas; having ground each separately and mixed in unadulterated wine and brought it to the boil, pour it over so that it is kneaded in due measure; then grind until it is dried; and having melted 50 drachmas of wax, 30 drachmas of terebinth resin of the pine, 8 kotylai of myrtle oil, mix 20 drachmas of the dry [ingredients] with the cerate. And this drug has none of the softening agents; however, in the mixing with the cerate, the one trained in reasoning by the methods I have set out would suitably work out the quantity of the mixture appropriate for each of the ulcers. And rightly too he wrote 'unadulterated wine', that is, wine with which sea-water has not been mixed...

...the meltable [ingredients], having let them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ones over these, stirring carefully. One must have ready, ground with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium, opopanax; and into these are put the things in the dish, and they are ground so that lumps of wax do not form. When it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box, having first smeared it with iris oil. On the third kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, about which Asclepiades wrote word for word as follows: 'In the case of ulcers that do not come together at all, or that come together but are dissolved again, either the flesh being corrupted or even the underlying bones having decayed, one must use the preparations set out below. For chironian and hard-to-heal [ulcers], a well-tried drug: of scale of copper and of scraped verdigris, 1 ounce each; of wax half a litra; of larch resin of the pine 1 ounce and a half. Pour the meltable [ingredients] over the dry ones, and having taken it up, use it, kneading carefully and applying a small flat piece upon...'

...the metallic [ingredients] with vinegar, and after these adding the dry ones and triturating again; then, when these have a clay-like consistency, mixing in the meltable ones, as has been said before. Another: of bitumen and terebinth resin of the pine and Bruttian pitch, 1 litra each; of oil 24 drachmas; of litharge and white lead and manna and verdigris and scale and opopanax, each equal to the twenty-four drachmas of the oil; of ladanum two ounces, which is 16 drachmas; and two kotylai of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another: of chrysocolla and scale and stomoma, 4 drachmas each; of verdigris and chalcanthum, half of each, that is 2 drachmas each; of wax 25 drachmas, that is 3 ounces and one drachma; of terebinth resin of the pine 2 ounces, that is 16 drachmas. Melt the wax with the terebinth...

Of verdigris of copper and of Indian aloe, of burnt copper and of good diphryges, sixteen and a half from each ingredient; twenty drachmas and 4 of the resinous juice of all-heal; of manna of frankincense the equal, twice 12; of ammoniac twice 5 and twice 20; sixteen drachmas of Attic propolis; of long aristolochia twice 10 drachmas; twice 6 drachmas of scale of Cyprian copper, and an equal amount of the driest root of gentian. To all these add further 20 holkai of dry dittany herb having its flower, finely ground. Putting litharge with oil into a new wide-mouthed earthenware dish, boil over a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it acquires the thickness of Attic honey; and adding again an equal amount of the scale, boil more fiercely; then, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, making the drug non-staining and set. Add the wax and the...

...of wax, having neither of these, but the ammoniac incense alone, when put in, will make the drug dry and harsh; but for plaster-making - for it is no worse to name it so - both the wax and the resin of the pine are useful. For softening and dispersing belong to the drug through the ammoniac alone, which holds first place among the emollient agents and is a rival also to the dispersive ones. And having recalled what was said in the fifth book of The Powers of Simple Drugs, as to what sort of mixture such drugs must have, you will need no further new instruction. For the primary powers that are active in drugs lie in heat and cold and moistness and dryness; the secondary are the emollient, dispersive, repellent, attractive, concocting, cleansing and septic, just as also...

...of all [ingredients] carefully; again let a little drip off; if you see it well-coloured and well-blended, lift the pot at once from the fire and add the resinous juice of all-heal, softened beforehand. But if the drug is harder by far, add oil to it for a good blending. Having strained it thus, then into another vessel; knead it cold with the hands, and so store it away. I shall set down another of the same kind as the one before it. It acts on the affections I mentioned before; this one cicatrizes better than all drugs ulcers hard to heal and callous and chronic; the eruptions that arise on the face this one cures without any bad biting; and seats that have fissures and hardnesses, the condylomatous ones, and it casts off calluses. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge - a mina is a litra and a third part of a litra; of good Pontic wax half a mina; of verdigris a fourth part of a mina, good scraped...

...scrofulous swellings, reducing every oedema, and healing the watery conditions of the liver and of the spleen, bringing on copious excretions of urine; it also resolves sciaticas that have become chronic. Using this, Ulpianus, a gifted young man, benefited very many. It contains one litra of Pontic wax, one of roasted [resin] and one of pine resin, 1 ounce of fresh quicklime, 1 ounce of split alum, and, equal to one of these, Pontic arsenic. Having poured a little fragrant vinegar over these, grind for a sufficient time in a larger mortar; and having added to wax and resin of the pine a little oil, melting it over the fierce flame of a fire, and mixing all carefully, and making malagmata of a non-staining thickness, keep it stored, using it, in the cases where it is needed, with a fresh compress. And the most excellent man, the father of the drug, said that also for deliverance from long diseases...

...which also heal small inflammations. Of the compound emollient drugs, some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first rank; some are not much stronger than these, in the second; and certain others in the third, and besides them yet others in the fourth. One should use, as has been said before, for slight hardnesses and soft bodies those of the first rank; for bodies and affections stronger than these, those of the second, just as also those of the third and the fourth, proportionally. And they also set down separately those under each of them. Emollient drugs of the first rank: butter, or the Colophonian resin of the pine, and white wax not old, the three equal in weight, melted together with one another, are emollient of the first rank; and the moist [cerate], when it is fresh...
